claim: The axolotl can regenerate multiple organs, including the brain.
source: The axolotl can regenerate multiple organs, including the brain.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Upon mechanical injury to the adult pallium, axolotls can regenerate several of the populations of neurons present before injury.
source: Here, we demonstrate that, upon mechanical injury to the adult pallium, axolotls can regenerate several of the populations of neurons present before injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing regeneration of molecularly defined neuronal subtypes (Figures 3, 5).

claim: Regenerated neurons acquire functional electrophysiological traits.
source: Notably, regenerated neurons acquire functional electrophysiological traits and respond appropriately to afferent inputs.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings showing action potentials and synaptic currents in regenerated neurons (Figure 4).

claim: Regenerated neurons respond appropriately to afferent inputs.
source: Notably, regenerated neurons acquire functional electrophysiological traits and respond appropriately to afferent inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by recordings of spontaneous postsynaptic currents in regenerated neurons (Figure 4f-g).

claim: Newborn neurons organize within altered tissue architecture after regeneration.
source: Despite the ability to regenerate specific, molecularly-defined neuronal subtypes, we also uncovered previously unappreciated limitations by showing that newborn neurons organize within altered tissue architecture and fail to re-establish the long-distance axonal tracts and circuit physiology present before injury.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of neuronal disorganization showing neurons in atypical radial positions (Figure 5a-b).

claim: Regenerated neurons fail to re-establish the long-distance axonal tracts present before injury.
source: Despite the ability to regenerate specific, molecularly-defined neuronal subtypes, we also uncovered previously unappreciated limitations by showing that newborn neurons organize within altered tissue architecture and fail to re-establish the long-distance axonal tracts and circuit physiology present before injury.
evidence: This is demonstrated by retrograde tracing showing reduced numbers of neurons projecting to the olfactory bulb (Figure 6a-b) and DTI showing disrupted fiber tracts (Figure 6d).

claim: Regenerated neurons fail to re-establish the circuit physiology present before injury.
source: Despite the ability to regenerate specific, molecularly-defined neuronal subtypes, we also uncovered previously unappreciated limitations by showing that newborn neurons organize within altered tissue architecture and fail to re-establish the long-distance axonal tracts and circuit physiology present before injury.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular field recordings showing decreased presynaptic fiber volley and field population spike amplitudes (Figure 7c-d).

claim: Under physiological conditions, the neurogenic capacity of the adult mammalian brain is largely restricted to two neurogenic niches.
source: Under physiological conditions, the neurogenic capacity of the adult mammalian brain is largely restricted to two neurogenic niches, the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricle, which gives rise to interneurons of the olfactory bulb and the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus, which generates granule cells of the hippocampus (Ming and Song, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ming and Song, 2011.

claim: The subventricular zone of the lateral ventricle gives rise to interneurons of the olfactory bulb.
source: Under physiological conditions, the neurogenic capacity of the adult mammalian brain is largely restricted to two neurogenic niches, the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricle, which gives rise to interneurons of the olfactory bulb and the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus, which generates granule cells of the hippocampus (Ming and Song, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Ming and Song, 2011.

claim: The subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus generates granule cells of the hippocampus.
source: Under physiological conditions, the neurogenic capacity of the adult mammalian brain is largely restricted to two neurogenic niches, the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricle, which gives rise to interneurons of the olfactory bulb and the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus, which generates granule cells of the hippocampus (Ming and Song, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Ming and Song, 2011.

claim: Neurons in other brain regions are only generated during embryonic development and are not replaced postnatally in mammals.
source: Neurons in other brain regions are only generated during embryonic development and are not replaced postnatally.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian neurogenesis.

claim: Urodele amphibians like the axolotl are endowed with the capacity to add new neurons to the brain throughout life.
source: Among these, urodele amphibians like the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) are endowed with the capacity to add new neurons to the brain throughout life (Maden et al., 2013) and can regenerate the spinal cord and parts of the brain after mechanical injury (Burr, 1916; Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964a; Butler and Ward, 1967; Piatt, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maden et al., 2013.

claim: Axolotls can regenerate the spinal cord and parts of the brain after mechanical injury.
source: Among these, urodele amphibians like the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) are endowed with the capacity to add new neurons to the brain throughout life (Maden et al., 2013) and can regenerate the spinal cord and parts of the brain after mechanical injury (Burr, 1916; Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964a; Butler and Ward, 1967; Piatt, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Burr, 1916; Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964a; Butler and Ward, 1967; Piatt, 1955.

claim: Resection of the middle one-third of one hemisphere, but not the whole hemisphere, in the axolotl telencephalon results in reconstruction of the injured hemisphere to a similar length as the contralateral, uninjured side.
source: Resection of the middle one-third of one hemisphere, but not the whole hemisphere, in the axolotl telencephalon results in reconstruction of the injured hemisphere to a similar length as the contralateral, uninjured side (Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964a; Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964b; Winkelmann and Winkelmann, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964a; Kirsche and Kirsche, 1964b; Winkelmann and Winkelmann, 1970.

claim: After mechanical excision of the newt optic tectum, new tissue fills the space produced by injury.
source: Similarly, after mechanical excision of the newt optic tectum, new tissue fills the space produced by injury (Okamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okamoto et al., 2007.

claim: In the newt, selective chemical ablation of dopaminergic neurons within a largely intact midbrain triggers regeneration of the ablated pool of neurons.
source: Interestingly, in the newt, selective chemical ablation of dopaminergic neurons within a largely intact midbrain triggers regeneration of the ablated pool of neurons (Berg et al., 2010; Parish et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berg et al., 2010; Parish et al., 2007.

claim: The axolotl pallium contains molecularly diverse neuronal populations.
source: The axolotl pallium contains molecularly diverse neuronal populations
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry showing expression of multiple neuronal subtype markers (Figure 1c-d).

claim: The neuronal composition of the axolotl pallium is largely unknown.
source: The neuronal composition of the axolotl pallium is largely unknown, with the urodele pallium being classically divided into medial pallium (MP), dorsal pallium (DP), and lateral pallium (LP) based on the size and location of cell nuclei, as well as rudimentary connectivity (Herrick, 1948; Kokoros and Northcutt, 1977; Westhoff and Roth, 2002) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to Herrick, 1948; Kokoros and Northcutt, 1977; Westhoff and Roth, 2002.

claim: The urodele pallium is classically divided into medial pallium (MP), dorsal pallium (DP), and lateral pallium (LP) based on the size and location of cell nuclei, as well as rudimentary connectivity.
source: The neuronal composition of the axolotl pallium is largely unknown, with the urodele pallium being classically divided into medial pallium (MP), dorsal pallium (DP), and lateral pallium (LP) based on the size and location of cell nuclei, as well as rudimentary connectivity (Herrick, 1948; Kokoros and Northcutt, 1977; Westhoff and Roth, 2002) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Herrick, 1948; Kokoros and Northcutt, 1977; Westhoff and Roth, 2002.

claim: Nine genes (ctip2, satb2, tle4, rorb, er81, fezf2, gad2, sst, and calb2) could be detected reliably in the axolotl pallium.
source: Among all markers tested, expression of nine genes could be detected reliably in the axolotl pallium: ctip2, satb2, tle4, rorb, er81, fezf2, gad2, sst, and calb2.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization experiments performed in the study.

claim: In the mouse neocortex, Fezf2 and Ctip2 are specifically expressed by subcerebral projection neurons (ScPNs) in layer Vb at high levels and by corticothalamic projection neurons (CThPNs) in layer VI at low levels.
source: In the mouse neocortex, Fezf2 and Ctip2 are specifically expressed by subcerebral projection neurons (ScPNs) in layer Vb at high levels and by corticothalamic projection neurons (CThPNs) in layer VI at low levels (Arlotta et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005a; Chen et al., 2005b; Molyneaux et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Arlotta et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005a; Chen et al., 2005b; Molyneaux et al., 2005.

claim: Er81 labels ScPNs but not CThPNs in the mouse neocortex.
source: Within these two neuronal populations, Er81 labels ScPNs (Yoneshima et al., 2006), but not CThPNs, which selectively express Tle4 (Molyneaux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Yoneshima et al., 2006.

claim: CThPNs selectively express Tle4 in the mouse neocortex.
source: Within these two neuronal populations, Er81 labels ScPNs (Yoneshima et al., 2006), but not CThPNs, which selectively express Tle4 (Molyneaux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Molyneaux et al., 2007.

claim: Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) across all layers distinctly express Satb2 and are negative for Ctip2, Fezf2, and Tle4 in the mouse neocortex.
source: Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) across all layers distinctly express Satb2 and are negative for Ctip2, Fezf2, and Tle4 (Alcamo et al., 2008; Britanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Alcamo et al., 2008; Britanova et al., 2008.

claim: Rorb labels locally connected excitatory interneurons of layer IV in the mouse neocortex.
source: Finally, Rorb labels locally connected excitatory interneurons of layer IV (Jabaudon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Jabaudon et al., 2012.

claim: Sst and Calb2 mark specific subtypes of Gad2+ cortical GABAergic interneurons in the mouse.
source: Among Gad2+ cortical GABAergic interneurons, Sst and Calb2 mark specific subtypes (Bartolini et al., 2013), although Calb2 has been shown to also be transiently expressed in pyramidal neurons residing in layer Va (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bartolini et al., 2013.

claim: Calb2 is transiently expressed in pyramidal neurons residing in layer Va in the mouse.
source: Among Gad2+ cortical GABAergic interneurons, Sst and Calb2 mark specific subtypes (Bartolini et al., 2013), although Calb2 has been shown to also be transiently expressed in pyramidal neurons residing in layer Va (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Ctip2 was highly expressed in DP with lower expression in MP and LP in the axolotl pallium.
source: Ctip2 was highly expressed in DP with lower expression in MP and LP
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Satb2 was expressed in a restricted region of DP and in scattered cells within MP in the axolotl pallium.
source: Satb2, detected by immunohistochemistry, was expressed in a restricted region of DP and in scattered cells within MP
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: tle4 marked a domain at the border of the dorso-lateral pallium and was expressed at lower levels across DP and MP in the axolotl.
source: tle4 marked a domain at the border of the dorso-lateral pallium and was expressed at lower levels across DP and MP
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The dorso-lateral pallium contains Satb2HI, Ctip2LO, Tle4HI cells and Satb2LO, Ctip2HI, Tle4HI cells in the axolotl.
source: We found that the dorso-lateral pallium contains Satb2HI, Ctip2LO, Tle4HI cells and Satb2LO, Ctip2HI, Tle4HI cells (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Satb2HI cells in the dorso-lateral pallium also express Calb2 in the axolotl.
source: Additionally, Satb2HI cells in the dorso-lateral pallium also express Calb2 (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The wound closes by 4 weeks post injury in the axolotl pallium.
source: We found that the wound closes by 4wpi, and is largely undetectable by 11wpi (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on stereoscope photographs of injured brains shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The wound is largely undetectable by 11 weeks post injury in the axolotl pallium.
source: We found that the wound closes by 4wpi, and is largely undetectable by 11wpi (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on stereoscope photographs of injured brains shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The sizes of the injury site remain unchanged for the first 14 days post-injury.
source: The sizes of the injury site (in mm3, see Materials and methods) remain unchanged for the first 14 days, but decrease rapidly within a subsequent four-day period (n=3).
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI measurements shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The sizes of the injury site decrease rapidly within a four-day period after the first 14 days post-injury.
source: The sizes of the injury site (in mm3, see Materials and methods) remain unchanged for the first 14 days, but decrease rapidly within a subsequent four-day period (n=3).
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI measurements shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Wound healing occurs largely by dynamic tissue remodeling that occurs before cellular proliferation starts.
source: This indicates that wound healing occurs largely by dynamic tissue remodeling that occurs before cellular proliferation starts.
evidence: This is inferred from the MRI data showing wound closure between 2-4wpi (Figure 2c-e) and BrdU labeling showing limited proliferation in the first 2 weeks (Figure 2g).

claim: At 4 weeks post injury, a large number of BrdU+/NeuN- cells populated the injured hemisphere.
source: At 4wpi, a large number of BrdU+/NeuN- cells populated the injured hemisphere, indicating that accumulation of proliferative cells precedes neuronal differentiation (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Accumulation of proliferative cells precedes neuronal differentiation in the regenerating axolotl pallium.
source: At 4wpi, a large number of BrdU+/NeuN- cells populated the injured hemisphere, indicating that accumulation of proliferative cells precedes neuronal differentiation (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of BrdU+/NeuN- cells at 4wpi and BrdU+/NeuN+ cells at 11wpi.

claim: BrdU+ cells expressed Sox2 and Gfap at 4 weeks post injury.
source: Of note, BrdU+ cells expressed Sox2 and Gfap, two ependymoglia cell markers (Kirkham et al., 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By 11 weeks post injury, the majority of BrdU+ cells expressed NeuN (69.5%, n=6 animals).
source: By 11wpi, the majority of BrdU+ cells expressed NeuN (69.5%, n=6 animals) (Figure 2i) indicating that neuronal differentiation occurs between 4 and 11wpi.
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Neuronal differentiation occurs between 4 and 11 weeks post injury in the regenerating axolotl pallium.
source: By 11wpi, the majority of BrdU+ cells expressed NeuN (69.5%, n=6 animals) (Figure 2i) indicating that neuronal differentiation occurs between 4 and 11wpi.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of BrdU+/NeuN- cells at 4wpi and BrdU+/NeuN+ cells at 11wpi.

claim: An injury to the pallium leads to generation of newborn neurons in the rostral telencephalon, a region distal to the injury site.
source: Quantification revealed that there were significantly more BrdU+/NeuN+ nuclei in the rostral telencephalon of injured animals compared to sham animals, indicating that an injury to the pallium leads to generation of newborn neurons distally (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on quantification of BrdU+/NeuN+ cells in the rostral telencephalon shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Regeneration of the pallium initiates with distinct morphological changes to the injury edge (stump), which thins out and closes the wound.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that regeneration of the pallium initiates with distinct morphological changes to the injury edge (stump), which thins out and closes the wound.
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI data showing stump formation, protrusion, and wound closure (Figure 2c-e).

claim: The progenitor proliferative response induced by injury is not restricted to the region immediately adjacent to the injury site but induces a more global response in distal uninjured regions.
source: In addition, the progenitor proliferative response induced by injury is not restricted to the region immediately adjacent to the injury site but induces a more global response in distal uninjured regions.
evidence: This is based on observations of increased BrdU+ and PH3+ cells in the rostral telencephalon (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: There are no significant differences between the number of NeuN+, Ctip2+, Satb2+, Tle4+, and Calb2+ neurons in the contralateral, injured (regenerated), and sham hemispheres at 11 weeks post injury.
source: From this analysis, we found no significant differences between the number of cells present in the contralateral, injured (regenerated), and sham hemispheres for any of the markers quantified (Figure 3b–f).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3b-f.

claim: The regenerated pallium contains each neuronal population in numbers comparable to control (contralateral and sham) pallium.
source: The data indicate that the regenerated pallium contains each neuronal population in numbers comparable to control (contralateral and sham) pallium.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantification showing no significant differences in neuronal subtype numbers (Figure 3b-f).

claim: The injury significantly increases the number of newborn neurons within each molecularly defined neuronal subpopulation at 11 weeks post injury, compared to controls.
source: This analysis showed that the injury significantly increases the number of newborn neurons within each molecularly defined neuronal subpopulation, compared to controls (n=6 contralateral; n=6 injured; n=4 sham) (Figure 3g–k and Table 1), indicating that distinct neuronal populations are regenerated upon injury.
evidence: This is based on quantification of BrdU+/neuronal marker+ cells shown in Figure 3g-k and Table 1.

claim: Distinct neuronal populations are regenerated upon injury to the axolotl pallium.
source: This analysis showed that the injury significantly increases the number of newborn neurons within each molecularly defined neuronal subpopulation, compared to controls (n=6 contralateral; n=6 injured; n=4 sham) (Figure 3g–k and Table 1), indicating that distinct neuronal populations are regenerated upon injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased BrdU+/neuronal marker+ cells in the injured hemisphere.

claim: Adult pre- and post-metamorphosis axolotls are able to regenerate neuronal subtypes within the dorsal pallium.
source: Together, these data show that adult pre- and post-metamorphosis axolotls are able to regenerate neuronal subtypes within the dorsal pallium.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data showing BrdU+/neuronal marker+ cells in post-metamorphosis axolotls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Injected, depolarizing current steps evoked action potentials in all cells recorded in the regenerated pallium.
source: Injected, depolarizing current steps evoked action potentials in all cells recorded in the regenerated pallium (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Regenerated neurons exhibited passive and active membrane properties that were comparable to those of control neurons.
source: We found that regenerated neurons exhibited passive and active membrane properties that were comparable to those of control neurons (Figure 4e and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4e and Table 2.

claim: In some cases, newly regenerated neurons displayed passive and active membrane properties indicative of a slightly immature state.
source: However, in some cases (2/14 neurons), when compared with uninjured neurons, newly regenerated neurons displayed passive and active membrane properties indicative of a slightly immature state, such as a larger Rm, a smaller Cm, more depolarized resting membrane potential, and broader and shorter action potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The regenerated pallium contained neurons of varying maturity.
source: These results indicate that the regenerated pallium contained neurons of varying maturity, but a large number of regenerated neurons were able to acquire mature electrophysiological traits comparable to endogenous control neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most (12/14) regenerated neurons had mature properties while some (2/14) showed immature properties.

claim: A large number of regenerated neurons were able to acquire mature electrophysiological traits comparable to endogenous control neurons.
source: These results indicate that the regenerated pallium contained neurons of varying maturity, but a large number of regenerated neurons were able to acquire mature electrophysiological traits comparable to endogenous control neurons.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements showing comparable properties in 12/14 regenerated neurons (Figure 4e, Table 2).

claim: All EdU+, regenerated neurons in the injured pallium received postsynaptic currents.
source: We found that all EdU+, regenerated neurons in the injured pallium received postsynaptic currents (Figure 4f) and displayed no differences in postsynaptic response compared to control neurons in the uninjured pallium (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is based on voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Regenerated neurons displayed no differences in postsynaptic response compared to control neurons in the uninjured pallium.
source: We found that all EdU+, regenerated neurons in the injured pallium received postsynaptic currents (Figure 4f) and displayed no differences in postsynaptic response compared to control neurons in the uninjured pallium (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is based on quantification of spontaneous postsynaptic current features shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Most of the spontaneous currents were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist, NBQX.
source: Most of the spontaneous currents were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist, NBQX, suggesting that AMPA receptors were involved in the synaptic transmission (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: AMPA receptors were involved in the synaptic transmission in regenerated neurons.
source: Most of the spontaneous currents were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist, NBQX, suggesting that AMPA receptors were involved in the synaptic transmission (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NBQX blocks most spontaneous currents.

claim: There are no significant differences in calcium transient characteristics (peak amplitude, rise time, and fall time) between uninjured and injured dorsal pallium neurons.
source: Measuring the key characteristics of spontaneously generated calcium transients, including the peak amplitude, rise time, and fall time, we detected no significant differences between uninjured (n=5 animals) and injured (11-15wpi; n=4 animals) dorsal pallium neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Video 2–3).
evidence: This is based on ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The regenerated neurons are able to mature into electrophysiologically functional neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that the regenerated neurons are able to mature into electrophysiologically functional neurons and to receive and respond locally to afferent inputs from other neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing action potentials, synaptic currents, and calcium transients in regenerated neurons.

claim: Regenerated neurons are able to receive and respond locally to afferent inputs from other neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that the regenerated neurons are able to mature into electrophysiologically functional neurons and to receive and respond locally to afferent inputs from other neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of spontaneous postsynaptic currents in regenerated neurons.

claim: In uninjured animals, bin 3 (closest to pia) is mostly populated by neuronal processes and does not contain cell bodies.
source: In uninjured animals, bin 3 is mostly populated by neuronal processes and does not contain cell bodies.
evidence: This is based on the observation that virtually no NeuN+ neurons are present in bin 3 in contralateral and sham hemispheres.

claim: Virtually no NeuN+ neurons are present within bin 3 in the contralateral and sham hemispheres.
source: In agreement, we found that virtually no NeuN+ neurons are present within this bin in the contralateral and sham hemispheres.
evidence: This is based on quantification of NeuN+ neurons shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: In the regenerated pallium at 11 weeks post injury, neurons are consistently found in bin 3.
source: However, in the regenerated pallium at 11wpi, we consistently found neurons in bin 3 (Contra n=7 DI 19.46 ± 3.272; Injured n=7 DI 212.4 ± 65.85; Sham n=5 DI 22.95 ± 8.508), indicating that the radial organization of neurons in the dorsal pallium at 11wpi is disrupted compared to controls (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is based on quantification of the disorganization index shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: The radial organization of neurons in the dorsal pallium at 11 weeks post injury is disrupted compared to controls.
source: However, in the regenerated pallium at 11wpi, we consistently found neurons in bin 3 (Contra n=7 DI 19.46 ± 3.272; Injured n=7 DI 212.4 ± 65.85; Sham n=5 DI 22.95 ± 8.508), indicating that the radial organization of neurons in the dorsal pallium at 11wpi is disrupted compared to controls (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of neurons in bin 3 in the injured hemisphere but not in controls.

claim: Neuronal disorganization remains present at 20 weeks post injury and is a stable feature of the regenerated pallium.
source: Similar to the 11wpi time point, neurons were consistently positioned in bin 3 in the injured hemisphere, but not in the control (Contra n=5 DI 40.87 ± 9.746; Injured n=5 DI 548.6 ± 104.1) (Figure 5a–b), indicating that neuronal disorganization remains present at 20wpi and is a stable feature of the regenerated pallium.
evidence: This is based on quantification of the disorganization index at 20wpi shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: The topography of neuronal subtypes is disorganized in the regenerated pallium.
source: The data prompted the question of whether the topography of neuronal subtypes is disorganized in the regenerate. We thus performed immunohistochemistry for Ctip2, Satb2, Tle4, and Calb2 at 20wpi. We found that, while the uninjured contralateral hemisphere showed stereotyped organization, in which neuronal subtypes cluster within distinct domains (Figure 5c, top panels), the dorsal pallium of the injured hemisphere contained neuronal subtypes localized outside of their stereotyped domains (Figure 5c, bottom panels).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The injured pallium contained scattered neuronal processes that lacked the stereotypical, circumscribed organization along the pia seen in the uninjured pallium.
source: In agreement, immunohistochemistry for Tubb3 in the dorsal pallium of 11wpi contralateral, injured, and sham hemispheres showed that the injured pallium contained scattered neuronal processes that lacked the stereotypical, circumscribed organization along the pia seen in the uninjured pallium (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry for Tubb3 shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The molecular diversity of neuronal subtypes is rebuilt within an altered pallial architecture.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the molecular diversity of neuronal subtypes is rebuilt within an altered pallial architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that neuronal subtypes are regenerated but their spatial organization is disrupted.

claim: In amphibians, neurons in the dorsal pallium project to the medial pallium (MP), lateral pallium (LP), and olfactory bulb (OB).
source: In amphibians, tracing studies have shown that neurons in the dorsal pallium project to the medial pallium (MP), lateral pallium (LP), and olfactory bulb (OB) (Westhoff and Roth, 2002; Northcutt et al., 1980; Neary et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Westhoff and Roth, 2002; Northcutt et al., 1980; Neary et al., 1990.

claim: A reduced number of neurons were retrogradely traced from the OB in the regenerated versus control axolotls.
source: We found that a reduced number of neurons were retrogradely traced from the OB in the regenerated versus control axolotls (Uninjured n=5 81.60 ± 13.90 neurons; 11wpi n=6 24.83 ± 5.326 neurons; 42wpi n=3 19.33 ± 2.603 neurons) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Regenerated BrdU+/Retrobead+ neurons accounted for only 10.2% and 6.6% of the total number of OB-projecting neurons located in the DP at 11wpi and 42wpi, respectively.
source: Notably, regenerated BrdU+/Retrobead+ neurons accounted for only 10.2% and 6.6% of the total number of OB-projecting neurons located in the DP at 11wpi and 42wpi, respectively, suggesting that the majority of the axons extending from the regenerated pallium to the OB originate from pre-existing BrdU- neurons that were spared by the injury (Figure 6c, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on quantification of BrdU+/Retrobead+ neurons shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The majority of the axons extending from the regenerated pallium to the OB originate from pre-existing BrdU- neurons that were spared by the injury.
source: Notably, regenerated BrdU+/Retrobead+ neurons accounted for only 10.2% and 6.6% of the total number of OB-projecting neurons located in the DP at 11wpi and 42wpi, respectively, suggesting that the majority of the axons extending from the regenerated pallium to the OB originate from pre-existing BrdU- neurons that were spared by the injury (Figure 6c, arrowheads).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only a small percentage of OB-projecting neurons are BrdU+.

claim: There is a reduction in the number of Retrobead+ neurons in the lateral pallium at 11wpi and 42wpi, despite the fact that this region was not mechanically injured.
source: Interestingly, we also found a reduction in the number of Retrobead+ neurons in the lateral pallium, despite the fact that this region was not mechanically injured (Uninjured n=5 118.2 ± 38.96 neurons; 11wpi n=6 21.83 ± 4.629 neurons; 42wpi n=3 29.67 ± 10.35 neurons) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Magnetic resonance tractography revealed distinct three-dimensional fiber tracts connecting the pallium and the olfactory bulb in the control, contralateral hemisphere.
source: In agreement with our retrograde tracing results, magnetic resonance tractography revealed distinct three-dimensional fiber tracts connecting the pallium and the olfactory bulb in the control, contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is based on DTI data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Significant truncation of fiber tracts was observed in the regenerated hemisphere.
source: In striking contrast, we observed significant truncation of the same bundles in the regenerated hemisphere (Figure 6d, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on DTI data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Regeneration of the pallium does not remake long-distance projections present in the original brain.
source: These results show that regeneration of the pallium does not remake long-distance projections present in the original brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the retrograde tracing and DTI data showing reduced projections to the olfactory bulb.

claim: In both DP-to-LP and DP-to-MP connections, the amplitude of the pre-synaptic fiber volley (NP1) was significantly reduced in the injured pallium compared to controls.
source: We found that, in both DP-to-LP and DP-to-MP connections, the amplitude of the pre-synaptic fiber volley (a measure of the number of axons being activated by an electrical stimulus; Negative Peak 1 or NP1) was significantly reduced in the injured pallium compared to controls (DP-to-LP: Uninjured n=5 animals; Injured n=3 animals; DP-to-MP: Uninjured n=4 animals; Injured n=3 animals) (Figure 7c–d), indicating that the activity of presynaptic axons is altered upon regeneration due to a change in number or firing properties of axons.
evidence: This is based on extracellular field recordings shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: The activity of presynaptic axons is altered upon regeneration due to a change in number or firing properties of axons.
source: We found that, in both DP-to-LP and DP-to-MP connections, the amplitude of the pre-synaptic fiber volley (a measure of the number of axons being activated by an electrical stimulus; Negative Peak 1 or NP1) was significantly reduced in the injured pallium compared to controls (DP-to-LP: Uninjured n=5 animals; Injured n=3 animals; DP-to-MP: Uninjured n=4 animals; Injured n=3 animals) (Figure 7c–d), indicating that the activity of presynaptic axons is altered upon regeneration due to a change in number or firing properties of axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced fiber volley amplitude.

claim: The field population spike (fEPSP) of both LP and MP was significantly decreased in injured axolotls compared to controls upon dorsal pallium stimulation.
source: In accordance, we also observed that the field population spike (fEPSP) of both LP and MP was significantly decreased in injured axolotls compared to controls upon dorsal pallium stimulation (Figure 7c–d), indicating that the MP and LP are not functionally activated to the same extent in the regenerated brain versus controls.
evidence: This is based on extracellular field recordings shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: The MP and LP are not functionally activated to the same extent in the regenerated brain versus controls.
source: In accordance, we also observed that the field population spike (fEPSP) of both LP and MP was significantly decreased in injured axolotls compared to controls upon dorsal pallium stimulation (Figure 7c–d), indicating that the MP and LP are not functionally activated to the same extent in the regenerated brain versus controls.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of decreased field population spike amplitude.

claim: Despite the striking ability of axolotl to regenerate a diversity of neuronal subtypes that are electrophysiologically mature and receive local afferent inputs, newborn neurons cannot rebuild long-distance circuit.
source: The data indicate that despite the striking ability of axolotl to regenerate a diversity of neuronal subtypes that are electrophysiologically mature and receive local afferent inputs, newborn neurons cannot rebuild long-distance circuit, as was previously assumed.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing functional regenerated neurons but failed long-distance projections.

claim: The adult axolotl can regenerate the original neuronal diversity upon a large mechanical injury to the pallium.
source: Here, we found that, upon a large mechanical injury to the pallium, the adult axolotl can regenerate the original neuronal diversity.
evidence: This is based on data showing regeneration of multiple molecularly defined neuronal subtypes (Figure 3).

claim: Newborn neurons acquire intrinsic electrophysiological properties and process afferent input in a manner that is indistinguishable from the endogenous neurons in uninjured brains.
source: Notably, newborn neurons acquire intrinsic electrophysiological properties and process afferent input in a manner that is indistinguishable from the endogenous neurons in uninjured brains.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing comparable properties between regenerated and control neurons (Figure 4).

claim: The capacity to regenerate neuronal diversity is not lost after metamorphosis in axolotls.
source: It is also interesting that this capacity is not lost after metamorphosis, challenging the theory that, in this species, regeneration is partly linked to the maintenance of a paedomorphic state in adulthood (Kirsche et al., 1965).
evidence: This is based on data showing regeneration in post-metamorphosis axolotls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The adult axolotl brain is capable of regenerating a diversity of neurons that are electrophysiologically functional, even when a large region of the brain is removed.
source: These results indicate that, beyond instructing the birth of new neurons, the adult axolotl brain is capable of regenerating a diversity of neurons that in turn are electrophysiologically functional, even when a large region of the brain is removed.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing neuronal diversity regeneration and electrophysiological functionality.

claim: Axolotls possess only limited capacity to rebuild original tissue architecture after large deletions of the pallium.
source: We found that axolotls possess only limited capacity to rebuild original tissue architecture after large deletions of the pallium.
evidence: This is based on data showing neuronal disorganization in the regenerated pallium (Figure 5).

claim: There is an unexpected limitation to the capacity of newborn neurons to extend axons to original targets in distal brain regions.
source: In addition, we uncovered an unexpected limitation to the capacity of newborn neurons to extend axons to original targets in distal brain regions.
evidence: This is based on retrograde tracing and DTI data showing reduced long-distance projections (Figure 6).

claim: Early steps of wound closure involve the generation of thinner processes from a stump that directionally grow towards each other before fusing.
source: We found that early steps of wound closure involve the generation of thinner processes from a stump that directionally grow towards each other before fusing.
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI data showing stump formation, protrusion, and closure (Figure 2c-e).

claim: Morphogenetic movements may act as a signaling event to trigger cellular proliferation and accumulation of newborn, differentiated cells at the site of injury.
source: It is possible that, much like the limb, morphogenetic movements act as a signaling event to trigger cellular proliferation and accumulation of newborn, differentiated cells at the site of injury.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to limb regeneration.

claim: No major waves of migration of endogenous neurons reconstitute neuronal diversity in the regenerated dorsal pallium.
source: In support of this possibility, we did not observe major waves of neuronal migration from regions adjacent to the injury site, and the topography of neurons in these regions remains properly organized upon regeneration.
evidence: This is based on quantification showing no significant differences in neuronal subtype numbers in regions adjacent to the injury (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Activated ependymoglia cells are one of the major sources of injury-induced newborn neurons in the newt and zebrafish.
source: Activated ependymoglia cells are one of the major sources of injury-induced newborn neurons in the newt and zebrafish (Berg et al., 2010; Kroehne et al., 2011), and these cells may similarly be the main origin of newborn neurons in the axolotl pallium.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Berg et al., 2010; Kroehne et al., 2011.

claim: Ependymoglia cells may be the main origin of newborn neurons in the axolotl pallium.
source: Activated ependymoglia cells are one of the major sources of injury-induced newborn neurons in the newt and zebrafish (Berg et al., 2010; Kroehne et al., 2011), and these cells may similarly be the main origin of newborn neurons in the axolotl pallium.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to other species and observation of Sox2+/Gfap+ BrdU+ cells.

claim: Reprogramming of endogenous differentiated cells may contribute to the generation of new neurons in the axolotl pallium.
source: An alternative, yet not exclusive, possibility is that reprogramming of endogenous differentiated cells may contribute to the generation of new neurons.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: In the zebrafish retina, Mueller glia appears capable of generating new neurons upon retinal injury.
source: Such reprogramming events were reported, for example, in the zebrafish retina, where Mueller glia appears capable of generating new neurons upon retinal injury (Bernardos et al., 2007; Fausett and Goldman, 2006; Ramachandran et al., 2010; Thummel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bernardos et al., 2007; Fausett and Goldman, 2006; Ramachandran et al., 2010; Thummel et al., 2008.

claim: The results highlight previously unappreciated limits for what vertebrates are able to achieve when faced with the need to regenerate the most complex tissues.
source: In addition, the results highlight previously unappreciated limits for what vertebrates are able to achieve when faced with the need to regenerate the most complex tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of failed long-distance connectivity and altered tissue architecture despite neuronal diversity regeneration.

claim: The findings should help define concrete goals and expectations for cellular replacement outcomes in the central nervous system of mammals.
source: This should help define concrete goals and expectations for cellular replacement outcomes in the central nervous system of mammals.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of the findings.

claim: Adult axolotls used in the study were 15–18 cm in length.
source: Adult animals, 15–18 cm in length, were used for all experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The wound closure process occurs rapidly, between 2 and 4 weeks post injury.
source: This method demonstrated that the wound closure process occurs rapidly, between 2 and 4wpi (Figure 2c–e and Video 1).
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI data shown in Figure 2c-e and Video 1.

claim: The lateral pallium formed a stump, which subsequently thinned out before protruding towards the medial pallium and closing the gap generated by the injury.
source: Notably, the lateral pallium formed a stump, which subsequently thinned out before protruding towards the medial pallium and closing the gap generated by the injury (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on in vivo MRI data shown in Figure 2d.
